summary: Jesse Hassenger's Polygon Q&A prepares viewers for the Five Nights at Freddy's movie, which arrives in theaters and on Peacock after a long development. It covers the mid-credits scene, whether newcomers can follow the film, what longtime fans will get, and how scary it is for kids. It also points to the earlier knockoff Willy's Wonderland, starring Nicolas Cage.
one_line: A spoiler-light Polygon FAQ on the Five Nights at Freddy's movie covering its credits scene, accessibility for newcomers, fan expectations, kid-suitability, and the Willy's Wonderland knockoff.
key_facts: Warner Bros. bought the Five Nights at Freddy's movie rights in 2015, and the project moved to Blumhouse a couple of years later.
Game creator Scott Cawthon wrote and rewrote the script, while Gil Kenan (Monster House) and Chris Columbus signed on and left the project before Emma Tammi directed.
The film is released in theaters simultaneously with a Peacock streaming debut.
The movie has a brief mid-credits comic scene featuring YouTuber Cory DeVante "CoryxKenshin" Williams, but no true post-credits scene, only a brief audio-only Easter egg.
Producer Jason Blum said at a New York Comic Con Blumhouse panel that the company cracked the adaptation by deciding not to make it with new audiences in mind, but to please the fans.
The film mimics the first game's premise: Mike (Josh Hutcherson) is hired as overnight security guard at an abandoned Chuck E. Cheese-style arcade restaurant and encounters animatronics.

Newcomers may be confused because the backstory is parceled out awkwardly, characters' decisions don't always make sense, and there is as much family melodrama as scares, but this isn't due to missing fan-only information.
Some of the more complicated game lore has been stripped out, and fans may see less screen time than expected for Freddy, Bonnie, Chica, Foxy, and Carl the Cupcake.
The film is rated PG-13, unlike R-rated A Nightmare on Elm Street or Friday the 13th, and is less intense than PG-13 horror films The Ring or Drag Me to Hell.
The film has plentiful cheap music-sting jump scares and some junior-level gore, making it a harder PG-13 than the average superhero movie; the article suggests a 12 or 13 age cutoff.

Willy's Wonderland, a knockoff in which Nicolas Cage plays an overnight janitor at a haunted Chuck E. Cheese-type location, was released before the FNAF movie, with Cage's performance entirely dialogue-free.
